text: With the data loaded, it's tempting to open a blank page and start dragging fields around. That produces a report that looks assembled, not designed. The fix is the same discipline as planning the query -- sketch the layout first.

Three visuals cover this requirement completely. Two KPI cards up top -- total sales amount and total order count across all categories -- answer how things are doing overall, in the first half second of looking at the page. A bar chart on the left, sales by category, answers which categories are driving sales. And a table on the right -- category, sales, order count -- gives the exact detail behind both of those.

Why a bar chart and not a pie chart, even with only four categories? A pie chart encodes value as an angle, and comparing two wedge angles precisely is harder than comparing two bar lengths, even with just four wedges. A bar chart can also be sorted highest to lowest, instantly showing the ranking the Merchandising Manager will want to discuss -- a pie chart has no equivalent for that.

Why a flat table and not a matrix? A matrix earns its place when you're pivoting two dimensions against each other as rows and columns. This report only has one grouping dimension -- category -- so there's nothing to pivot against. A flat table is simpler to read and matches the one-row-per-category shape the query already produces.
And no line chart at all, because there's only one quarter of data here -- no series of periods, so nothing for a trend chart to actually show.
With the grid sketched on paper before touching the canvas, next lesson writes the DAX measures that will actually power these cards and this chart.
